title: A thoughtful welcome
text: Welcome to DigiStayBook. One QR display gives your guests a place to find house guidance, discover your local favourites and leave memories from their stay. A thoughtful welcome can start with something simple. Explore: https://digistaybook.com

title: Think like a tired traveller
text: Try reading your arrival instructions as if you've just stepped off a long flight. Is the entrance obvious? Is the key collection clear? A calm arrival starts with details guests can find quickly.

title: The Wi-Fi test
text: A useful Wi-Fi note needs both the network name and the password. Check the capital letters, test it on a phone and make the information easy to find. Small detail, welcome relief.

title: Recommend one good breakfast
text: A long list of cafes can leave guests with another decision to make. Start with one breakfast spot you know well and explain why you like it. Personal context makes a recommendation useful.

title: A place for the suitcase
text: Walk into your guest bedroom carrying a suitcase. Where would you open it? Somewhere practical to unpack can make a small room feel much easier to settle into.

title: A clear last morning
text: Checkout instructions are easiest to follow when guests can see them before the last morning. Put the time, key return and essential final steps together in one short note.

title: More than a rating
text: A guestbook can hold the small moments that don't fit into a star rating: a favourite walk, a family breakfast or a quiet evening on the deck. Those are the memories DigiStayBook is made for.

title: Answer the next question
text: Keep a note of the questions guests ask during each stay. If the same one comes up again, it's a good candidate for your house guidance. Let real questions shape the information you provide.

title: A visitor's version of your suburb
text: You know your neighbourhood by habit. A visitor doesn't. The nearest breakfast option, a simple walking route and one local favourite can help guests feel oriented sooner.

title: The repeat question
text: Hosts: what's the question you've answered so often you could type it with your eyes closed? Wi-Fi, parking, heating or something completely unexpected?

title: No guest app
text: Guests already have enough to organise when they travel. DigiStayBook opens in a browser, with no guest app to download and no guest account to create. See the idea in action: https://digistaybook.com/wall/demo-cottage

title: Photograph the right entrance
text: If your property has a side gate, shared driveway or entrance that doesn't face the street, a clear arrival photo can help. Show the route a first-time visitor will actually take.

title: Bin day in plain English
text: Instead of writing only 'bins Tuesday', explain which bin, where it goes and when to bring it back. Instructions that feel obvious to a local can be a puzzle to a visitor.

title: The rainy-day recommendation
text: Give guests an option for a wet afternoon as well as a sunny one. Think about something nearby that you would enjoy yourself, and remind visitors to check current opening times.

title: Make charging easy
text: Look at the room from the bed and sofa. Can a guest charge a phone without moving furniture? A clearly available power point is a practical part of a comfortable stay.

title: Keep the list proportionate
text: Read your checkout list from the guest's perspective. Keep the essential steps easy to spot and explain anything unusual. A short, clear finish can leave a warmer final impression.

title: Ask about a moment
text: A gentle guestbook prompt can be as simple as 'What was your favourite moment here?' It gives people a starting point without turning their holiday into a questionnaire.

title: One source for the basics
text: If checkout time appears in three different places, check that all three agree. Consistent information helps guests make plans and saves you from correcting mixed messages later.

title: Explain the local trip
text: When recommending a neighbourhood outing, say how guests might get there and what to check before leaving. A useful local tip helps with the journey as well as the destination.

title: Your smallest useful touch
text: What's the smallest thing you've added to a holiday rental that guests have noticed? A reading lamp, luggage stand, labelled switch or something else? We'd love to hear the practical ideas.

title: House guidance above the memories
text: DigiStayBook brings practical house information and guest memories together. Your guidance sits above the guest wall, so visitors can find the essentials before browsing the notes and photos. Explore: https://digistaybook.com

title: Check the arrival light
text: Visit your entrance after dark. Can you see the path, the door number and the key collection point? Your daytime arrival walkthrough may miss what an evening guest needs.

title: The appliance quick start
text: For an unfamiliar appliance, start with the few steps needed for normal use. Identify the relevant buttons and the usual setting. Keep the full manufacturer's instructions available for anything more detailed.

title: Say why you recommend it
text: A recommendation becomes more useful with a reason. 'Good for an early breakfast' or 'a quiet place for a walk' tells guests more than a name alone. Specific beats a copied list.

title: Check the reading light
text: A bright ceiling light and a useful reading light do different jobs. Try sitting where a guest might read in the evening and check whether the lighting feels comfortable there.

title: Key return without guesswork
text: Describe exactly where keys should go at checkout. If a lockbox is involved, explain the final step clearly. The end of the stay shouldn't depend on a last-minute message.

title: Make sharing optional
text: A guestbook invitation should feel like an invitation. Some guests will love leaving a photo or note; others will prefer a quiet stay. Both deserve the same warm welcome.

title: A ten-minute information audit
text: Before your next arrival, spend ten minutes checking the basics: access, Wi-Fi, heating, bins and checkout. Read the instructions against what is actually in the property today.

title: A recommendation for a short stay
text: A guest with one free afternoon needs different ideas from someone staying a week. Offer a small, realistic outing as well as the longer day trip. Time is part of the recommendation.

title: The first thing you check
text: When you arrive at a holiday rental yourself, what do you look for first? The Wi-Fi, a cup of tea, somewhere to unpack or the nearest place to eat?

title: A QR code with a purpose
text: A QR display is useful when guests know what it opens. DigiStayBook brings house guidance, local favourites and a guest wall into the browser. A short label beside the code can set that expectation.

title: The five-minute walkthrough
text: Start outside your property and follow your own check-in instructions on your phone. Notice every place where you rely on memory. Those are the details a new guest may need explained.

title: Label the surprising switch
text: If a switch does something a guest wouldn't expect, a clear label can help. Think outdoor lights, extractor fans and unusual heating controls. Good guidance starts with the small points of confusion.

title: Include a nearby easy option
text: Not every guest wants a big day out. Include something simple close to the property: a pleasant walk, an easy coffee stop or somewhere to sit outside. Useful can be wonderfully ordinary.

title: Give the bedside table a job
text: A bedside surface can hold a phone, a glass of water and a book. Check there is room for a guest's belongings alongside your decor. Practical space is part of feeling welcome.

title: Explain rather than surprise
text: If something at departure needs special care, tell guests early and explain it clearly. A surprise instruction on checkout morning is harder to plan around than a note available throughout the stay.

title: A photo can tell a small story
text: The most memorable guestbook photo doesn't need to be a perfect property photograph. It might be breakfast on the balcony or a favourite corner for reading. Encourage moments, with people's permission.

title: Use guest language
text: If guests call it 'the heater', make sure your instructions do too. Familiar words are easier to search for and understand than model numbers or the terminology from an installation manual.

title: Help guests choose their own pace
text: Some visitors want a full itinerary; others want one good walk and a slow breakfast. A small range of local ideas can welcome both without prescribing how a holiday should look.

title: Your favourite local recommendation
text: What's the local recommendation you're always happy to give a guest? It could be a bakery, a walking route or a quiet spot you think deserves more love.

title: Guests can leave a note
text: A short thank-you, a favourite discovery or a memory from the stay: DigiStayBook gives guests a place to leave their own words alongside your house guidance. Take a look: https://digistaybook.com/wall/demo-cottage

title: Say what happens next
text: After guests collect the keys, what should they do next? A simple instruction about the door, parking or where to find the welcome information can help an unfamiliar arrival feel straightforward.

title: Heating without a guessing game
text: Write down how to turn the heating on, how to adjust it and anything a guest should avoid changing. Check your directions against the controls in the room, not just the appliance name.

title: Keep your favourites current
text: A recommendation is worth revisiting occasionally. Check that the business still exists and that the link works. For hours, bookings and availability, point guests to the business's current information.

title: A welcome shelf, not a puzzle
text: If you provide tea, coffee or other welcome items, make them easy to find and explain what guests are welcome to use. A thoughtful touch works best when nobody has to guess.

title: Think about early departures
text: Would your checkout instructions still work for someone leaving before sunrise? Check lighting, key return and any access steps. An early departure deserves the same clarity as a daytime one.

title: Keep private details private
text: Before sharing a guest memory more widely, check permission and look for private information in the picture or words. A lovely moment doesn't need a booking number, door code or someone's travel plans attached.

title: Check from a phone
text: House guidance that looks neat on a laptop may feel long on a phone. Read it on the kind of screen guests will use. Put the most useful information where it is easy to spot.

title: Give context to a day trip
text: If you suggest a longer outing, help guests judge the time commitment. They can then decide whether it fits around their arrival, event or checkout plans. A recommendation should make planning easier.

title: The unexpected guest question
text: What's the most unexpected practical question a guest has asked you? Sometimes the question that surprises a host is exactly the one the next visitor will need answered too.

title: Host curation matters
text: DigiStayBook gives hosts tools to curate the guest wall, including pinning, hiding and deleting posts. A shared space for guest memories still needs a host's care and attention.

title: Separate access from the extras
text: Guests arriving with bags need the door instructions before the full neighbourhood guide. Put the information in the order they will use it. A welcome can unfold one useful step at a time.

title: Parking deserves a clear note
text: If you provide parking information, make the location and any property-specific instructions clear. Ask guests to check current signs and restrictions whenever they park elsewhere. Avoid leaving important details to assumption.

title: Think about different budgets
text: A useful local guide can include a simple picnic idea as well as a special meal. Give guests a few ways to enjoy the area without assuming everyone wants the same kind of spend.

title: Room for real belongings
text: Take a look at your shelves, hooks and benches. Is there space for a coat, a wash bag and a few personal things? A property can look styled and still leave room for the people staying in it.

title: The final message can be warm
text: A departure reminder can be clear and friendly at the same time. Put the practical steps first, thank guests for their stay and make it easy to ask about anything uncertain.

title: A guestbook is a different space
text: Official booking-platform reviews and a guestbook serve different purposes. DigiStayBook is a place for stay memories and practical guidance. Guests can choose whether they also leave feedback on their booking platform.

title: Refresh one section at a time
text: Updating your house information doesn't need to become a huge project. Pick one section, check it properly and move to the next. Small, regular improvements can keep the whole guide useful.

title: Plan for different weather
text: When guests ask for local ideas, offer an indoor option alongside the outdoor one. They can choose based on the day's conditions. A flexible suggestion is often more useful than a fixed itinerary.

title: What makes a welcome feel personal?
text: A handwritten line, a useful local tip, clear instructions or simply having everything where you expect it: what makes a holiday rental feel welcoming to you?

title: One dashboard for your properties
text: Managing more than one property means keeping each home's information straight. DigiStayBook brings properties into one host dashboard while giving each property its own QR kit and guest wall.

title: Use landmarks carefully
text: A landmark can help someone find an entrance, but check that it is still there and easy to recognise. Pair it with clear directions rather than relying on 'you'll know it when you see it'.

title: Put the contact route in writing
text: Make it clear how guests should contact the host for ordinary stay questions. Keep that route easy to find. A guestbook or house guide should complement the support you provide during the stay.

title: Describe the walk
text: If you recommend a walk, give guests a sense of its length, surface and any steps you know about. They can decide whether it suits them. 'Easy' can mean different things to different people.

title: Practical hooks help
text: A hook in the right place can be surprisingly useful: near the entrance, in a bedroom or beside the shower. Walk through the space imagining where a guest would naturally put things down.

title: Check every version of the time
text: If checkout time is in your listing, welcome message and house guide, make sure it matches. A quick consistency check is easier than resolving uncertainty on the morning someone leaves.

title: A prompt for the next visitor
text: Try a guestbook prompt such as 'What would you recommend to the next person staying here?' It can turn a personal discovery into a useful idea for someone else's trip.

title: Make a change when the house changes
text: New coffee machine? Different Wi-Fi details? A changed bin arrangement? Update the guest information at the same time. The guide is most useful when it reflects the property guests actually arrive at.

title: Start with your own neighbourhood
text: A visitor guide doesn't have to cover all of Melbourne. Your street, nearby shops and a few places you know personally can be a much more helpful starting point for someone new to the area.

title: Paper, digital or both?
text: How do you currently share house information with guests: a folder, a message, a digital guide or a mix? What works well, and what would you like to make easier?

title: Guest photos, with screening
text: Photos and messages submitted through DigiStayBook pass automated screening before publication, with flagged content waiting for host review. Moderation is part of looking after a guest wall. Product overview: https://digistaybook.com

title: A good welcome is findable
text: Even beautifully written information can't help if guests don't know where it is. Give the welcome information an obvious home and explain how to reach it. Finding the answer is part of the experience.

title: Laundry instructions in a few steps
text: If guests can use the laundry, explain the everyday cycle, where supplies are kept and how to dry things appropriately. A few practical lines can be more useful than an unexplained panel of symbols.

title: Recommend for a reason, not a commission
text: The most useful local recommendations start with the guest's needs. Explain what you personally like and disclose a commercial relationship if one is relevant. Trust is part of a good recommendation.

title: Check the bathroom from a guest's view
text: Is there somewhere for a wash bag? Can a towel hang properly? Is the light useful? The everyday routines of a stay deserve as much attention as the arrival photograph.

title: Make the last step unmistakable
text: After guests lock up, is there anything else they need to know? Put the final step plainly in your checkout note. A clear ending lets people leave with confidence.

title: The little moments count
text: A slow breakfast, a board game, the first cup of coffee outside: not every guestbook memory has to be a big adventure. Sometimes the small moments say the most about a stay.

title: Read your longest paragraph
text: Find the longest paragraph in your house guide. Could it become a short heading and three useful steps? Making information easier to scan can help guests find what they need while standing in the room.

title: An event trip is still a stay
text: Visitors coming for an event still need the everyday basics: arrival, breakfast, transport planning and checkout. Help with those first, then add the extra local ideas that make the trip feel personal.

title: The best thing a guest has taught you
text: Have guests ever shown you a better use for part of your property or recommended a local place you hadn't tried? Hosting can be a two-way exchange of useful discoveries.

title: Try the guest view
text: The easiest way to understand DigiStayBook is to look at a guest wall. Browse the demonstration property and see how house guidance and memories sit together. Demo: https://digistaybook.com/wall/demo-cottage

title: Write for the first visit
text: When checking arrival information, ask someone unfamiliar with the property to read it. Notice which words need explaining. A fresh pair of eyes can spot the details a host has stopped seeing.

title: Explain the outdoor space
text: If guests can use a courtyard, garden or balcony, explain any property-specific details they need. Keep shared areas and private areas clear. A short note can help people enjoy the space considerately.

title: One option for a quiet morning
text: Not every local recommendation needs a booking or a ticket. A pleasant route for a morning walk can be a useful addition to your guide. Explain where to start and what guests should check before setting off.

title: Useful information is hospitality
text: A guest shouldn't have to feel awkward about asking how something works. Clear house guidance is one way to make a place feel welcoming before a question is even asked.

title: Keep the departure route clear
text: During a changeover check, look at the route guests use to leave with bags. A clear path and straightforward instructions help the final few minutes feel as considered as the welcome.

title: A memory is not a marketing promise
text: Every stay is different. A guest's lovely note is their own experience, not a guarantee of what the next person will feel. Share memories thoughtfully and keep their context intact.

title: Choose a clear QR location
text: Place guest information where people can naturally find it, then test it from there. For a QR display, check the light, viewing distance and the short explanation beside it. Test on a phone before guests arrive.

title: Local knowledge without overload
text: Three useful recommendations with a sentence of context can be easier to use than thirty unexplained links. Start small, listen to guest questions and add detail where it helps.

title: What would you tell a first-time host?
text: If you could give a new holiday-rental host one practical tip about welcoming guests, what would it be? The everyday advice is often the most useful.

title: House information can feel welcoming
text: Wi-Fi details, checkout steps and local favourites don't have to feel like a list of warnings. DigiStayBook is built around making practical information part of a warmer guest experience. Explore: https://digistaybook.com

title: The arrival message check
text: Before sending arrival information, check the property name, dates and access details. Reusing a message is convenient; a quick final read helps make sure it fits this particular stay.

title: Give the unusual detail a heading
text: If your place has a quirk guests need to know about, give it a clear heading. Important information is easier to find when it isn't buried halfway through a general welcome paragraph.

title: Your guide can grow with experience
text: Start with the recommendations you can explain confidently. Add to them as you learn what guests enjoy and ask about. A local guide can be useful before it is extensive.

title: A comfortable stay has practical roots
text: A clear entrance, a useful light, somewhere for a bag and instructions that make sense: these details may be small individually, but together they help a guest settle in.

title: Leave room for a thank-you
text: Once the practical departure details are clear, a simple thank-you can finish the stay warmly. Hospitality doesn't need complicated wording. Clarity and kindness work well together.

title: A guestbook that stays with the home
text: One of the lovely things about a guestbook is the connection between different stays. A favourite walk or a small discovery can become part of the home's story for the next visitor.

title: Build from the real stay
text: The best guest information follows what happens in the property: arriving, settling in, using things, exploring and leaving. Organise your guidance around those moments and see where the gaps appear.

title: A home base for exploring
text: A holiday rental is both a place to stay and a starting point for discovering somewhere new. Clear house information helps with the first; thoughtful local tips can help with the second.

title: Help shape DigiStayBook
text: Hosts and holiday-rental owners: what would make your guest information easier to manage? We'd love to hear the everyday problems, the repeated questions and the small improvements that would help most. https://digistaybook.com
